rationale.totalSecondsMaximum: The render sandbox accepts at most SANDBOX_FRAMES_MAXIMUM (600) captured frames, so at framesPerSecond the longest admissible brand-motion film is 600 / 30 = 20 seconds. Declaring a larger total here would let a legal user configuration be refused by the sandbox as an opaque configuration error, which is why duration_limits() re-checks this product against the sandbox ceiling and fails closed.
rationale.beatCount: One beat is the smallest storyboard that still renders a film. Ten is the point where the total budget can no longer give every beat two seconds, so beyond it the editor would only be able to produce beats too short to read.
rationale.secondsPerBeat: One second is the shortest beat a viewer can read a title and a caption in. Ten seconds is half the whole budget: a single static template card held longer than that is a stall, not a shot.
rationale.defaults: Three beats of four seconds is a twelve second film. The retired template produced three seconds in total, which is shorter than any usable social clip; the default now lands inside the range every platform accepts while staying well under the total budget.
rationale.renderWall: Wall clock for a render is a fixed startup cost (browser launch, page load, warm-up stability probing) plus a per-frame cost (seek, composite, capture). Pinning it to one number meant a 90 frame render and a 600 frame render shared a 60 second budget, so the longest legal film would always be killed as a stall. At 30 + 0.4s per frame the longest film asks for 270 seconds, inside the 300 second sandbox ceiling.
rationale.renderCpuParallelism: CPU seconds are summed over the whole browser process tree, so a render occupying N cores accrues them N times faster than wall clock. motion-render-sandbox-budget.v1 measures a legitimate composition render at roughly 2-3 cores average and permits at most 8. Declaring 3 leaves that measured render room without a false runaway trip, and still keeps the guard at three eighths of the permitted ceiling.
rationale.twoCeilings:
totalSecondsMaximum and briefSecondsMaximum answer different questions and stopped being the same number when one of the two paths stopped being a single render. The fixed-template path still captures one composition in one pass, so its ceiling is the sandbox's 600 frames divided by framesPerSecond — raising it would produce a single 5400-frame capture the sandbox refuses. The one-sentence path is route A: one render per shot, each inside the sandbox's limit, joined afterwards. Its ceiling is therefore a product decision about how long a film the operator may ask for, and the product owner set it at 180 seconds on 2026-07-28. The reason was measured: at the previous fixed 12 seconds the model declined every catalog part as too expensive — the shortest part runs 4.5 seconds, 37% of that budget — so the 134 packaged parts were reachable in principle and never chosen in practice. A 20 second brief picked one to two parts.
What this ceiling does not remove is the cost: each shot is its own render with its own browser launch, so a long film is paid for per shot rather than per film. renderWallSecondsBase is that per-shot fixed cost and the submit screen has to show it.
rationale.briefBeats: The one-sentence path has no beat grid — the model cuts the film — so these two bound what it may be told to do. briefBeatCountMaximum is what write_storyboard accepts and is also a cost: one beat is one render, and every render pays renderWallSecondsBase again. briefSecondsPerBeatMinimum is the shortest beat a viewer can read a title and a caption in, the same floor secondsPerBeatMinimum gives the template editor. The suggested beat length handed to the model is derived from the two rather than fixed, because a fixed '2 to 3 seconds' and a 24 beat ceiling have no common solution past 72 seconds: the model either produces sixty beats that are refused, or ignores the suggestion. Both endings are the same for the operator — minutes of authoring, then a refusal, at a length the form offered him. duration_limits() also checks that a film at briefSecondsMaximum can be cut into at most briefBeatCountMaximum shots that each fit one capture.
